tagline.text: The heart of Vigan's old town, where an obelisk meets a dancing fountain

location.label: Location
location.text: Center of the historic district, Vigan City, Ilocos Sur (in front of Vigan Cathedral)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–300 (free entry; snacks and transport extra)

children.text: Plaza Salcedo is the central square of the UNESCO World Heritage city of Vigan, known for its 17th-century obelisk and an evening dancing fountain show. Surrounded by Vigan Cathedral and administrative buildings, it is free to enter and makes a good starting point for a walk through the old town.

Plaza Salcedo is a public park and square in the center of Vigan City, Ilocos Sur. According to Wikipedia, it is the longer arm of an L-shaped open space, and the shorter arm is Plaza Burgos. It is named after the Spanish conquistador Juan de Salcedo. Vigan was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999, and this plaza is the center of its grid-pattern town plan. Administrative and religious buildings stand close together around it, so it is the first spot most first-time visitors mark on their maps. Walk once around the plaza and you will see why the town hall, the cathedral and the archbishop's residence are so close: Spanish colonial towns were planned with a plaza at the center and the church and government buildings built around it. This plaza is a rare example of that principle still alive today.

In the middle of the plaza stands an obelisk said to date from the 17th century, surrounded by a moat-like pool. The pool is said to have been built in the 1970s to store water for firefighting, because fires were frequent in the town at the time. That means the plaza is not just a park but a space tied to the real life of the old town. The plaza also has statues of José Rizal and Elpidio Quirino and a provincial Ilocos Sur sign, and the tower of Vigan Cathedral rises behind it.

This is also a place of history. On September 20, 1763, the Spanish authorities are said to have hanged Gabriela Silang, who had taken up the revolt of her husband Diego Silang, in Vigan's central plaza. She is called the "Joan of Arc of Ilocandia." Earlier, on May 28, 1763, her husband Diego Silang was assassinated in Vigan by two of his former allies. Gabriela went on to lead the rebels but was captured in Abra and, according to tradition, was brought to Vigan and executed that September. She was 32. Keep this event, and the story of the Gomburza priests, in mind as you walk and the old town reads more deeply.

In the evening the mood of the plaza changes. The Vigan Dancing Fountain show, lit with colorful lights, draws local families and tourists. It is free and easy to reach on foot, so it works well as both the first and the last stop of a Vigan trip. This guide is for independent travelers and families spending a day or two in Vigan. Fountain schedules and events can change, so check local announcements before you visit. For visitors the plaza is a resting place, and for Vigan residents it is something like a shared living room. Children run around by the pool and adults sit on benches in the evening breeze. Sitting quietly and blending into that scene is the best experience the plaza offers.

The obelisk standing in the middle of the plaza is said to date from the 17th century. The pool around it is explained as having been built in the 1970s to store firefighting water, which ties it to the town's history of fires. By day it is a good spot to photograph the obelisk together with the cathedral.
The Department of Tourism’s
Dancing Fountain guide

describes the evening light-and-music show at Plaza Salcedo. Ask the local tourism office whether the show is running and when it starts on your date, since events and maintenance can affect the schedule.

The plaza is known as the place where Gabriela Silang was executed by the Spanish authorities in September 1763. Look at the memorials and markers around the plaza and think about the history of resistance in Ilocos.
The plaza has a statue of José Rizal and a monument to President Elpidio Quirino. Quirino, a president from Ilocos Sur, is a source of local pride. Many travelers take photos in front of the statues.

blocks.title: Vigan Cathedral and its bell tower

children.text: Right behind the plaza is Saint Paul Metropolitan Cathedral. According to Wikipedia, the present building was built between 1790 and 1800 in the Earthquake Baroque style, and the separate bell tower is about 25 m tall. It was badly damaged in the 2022 earthquake and repairs have continued, and its bells rang again in 2025. The parish began in 1574 with a temporary wood-and-thatch church built on the orders of Juan de Salcedo, and it became a cathedral in 1758 when the diocesan seat moved to Vigan.
Plaza Salcedo joins the shorter Plaza Burgos in an L shape. You can walk around both plazas and the cathedral in one loop, which makes it a handy reference point for finding your way in the old town.

blocks.title: A walking base in the old town

children.text: Old-town sights such as Padre Burgos House and Calle Crisologo are within walking distance. Starting from the plaza, you can tour the old town without a map app, and the kalesa (horse-drawn carriage) stop is close by.
Wikivoyage says the plaza is open
and free. A big advantage is that you can enjoy both a morning stroll and the evening fountain without any organized tour.

items.title: Half-day plaza-centered route
items.subtitle: From a morning stroll to the evening fountain

children.text: Walk around the pool in the morning and enjoy the obelisk and the cathedral quietly.
Walk to Padre Burgos House, a branch of the National Museum.
Step into the cathedral next to the plaza to see the altar and the wooden decoration. Areas under repair may be closed.
Have lunch of Vigan empanada or sinanglao at a restaurant near the plaza.
Walk the cobblestones and old houses of Calle Crisologo and take a kalesa ride.
Return to the plaza, take photos at sunset and wait for the fountain to start.
Watch the dancing fountain and finish at a cafe or snack shop at the edge of the plaza.
The plaza itself needs only
1–2 hours
. The rest of the day is walking time in the old town.

items.title: Two-day Vigan route
items.subtitle: The old town and the Bantay bell tower

children.text: Start at the plaza, go around the cathedral, the museum and Calle Crisologo, and watch the fountain in the evening.
Take a tricycle to the Bantay Church and bell tower area.
If you have time, head north toward Paoay Church.
Check the bus times back to Manila first.
Vigan is about 404 km from Manila, and the trip takes about
7–10 hours
by bus or car. Companies such as Partas, Dominion Bus Lines, Viron Transit and St. Joseph (Aniceto Transit) run the route.
Wikivoyage lists a Dominion fare of ₱580, but that figure dates from November 2017, so check the current fare when you book.
From the bus terminal to the plaza, take a short tricycle ride.
As of September 2023, Vigan's own airport reportedly had no scheduled flights. The nearest airport is Laoag International Airport (LAO), about
1 hour 30 minutes
away by car.
Flights between Manila and Laoag are reported to operate daily. Check the airline's timetable.
Wikivoyage lists tricycle fares within the city at about
, but they may have gone up, so confirm the fare.
A kalesa is described as costing about
per hour, or about
for a full day of 6–7 hours.
From the plaza, walking is enough to reach the old-town sights.
Vigan has a tropical savanna climate, with a dry season from about November to April and a wet season from May to October. The average temperature is about
. The plaza is outdoors, so bring an umbrella or light rain jacket in the rainy months, and a hat and water for the midday heat.

Vigan is reported to be hit by 7 to 10 typhoons a year, so check the forecast from August to October. Around New Year, during the Ilocos Sur Festival and at Christmas, the plaza gets crowded and accommodation fills up early.

items.label: Lodging (simple hotel)
items.note: Large differences by season and facilities

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.

Around the plaza and in the old town there are many hotels and guesthouses in restored old houses. Wikivoyage lists Vigan Hotel at about ₱500 for a double, Casa Teofila Lodge at about ₱1,079–1,476, Villa Angela Heritage House at about ₱1,500–2,800 and El Juliana Hotel at about ₱1,500. Prices change with the season, so check when you book. A place within walking distance of the plaza is the most convenient.
Typical food includes Vigan empanada, sinanglao, arroz caldo, miki and okoy. Wikivoyage lists Insiang's Empanada (
) and First Sinanglaoan (
). Vigan longganisa is spicy, unlike the Pampanga version.

A common evening plan is to watch the fountain and then move on to restaurants and cafes near Calle Crisologo. Opening hours differ from shop to shop, so check closing times in advance if you plan a late dinner. The plaza is surrounded by the town hall, the cathedral and old buildings, so by day you can alternate indoor sightseeing with meals.
The plaza is known to be open
, but hours may differ during events, so check on-site notices.
Check the fountain schedule locally.
Go early in the morning when it is quiet and photos come out clean.
There is little shade at midday, so bring a hat and water.
The cathedral was under repair after the 2022 earthquake, and its bells began ringing again in 2025. Check on site whether the interior is open.
Agree on the fare and route before you board a kalesa.
The cathedral bell tower is reported to ring on weekends at
and
. If you want to hear the bells, plan your visit around those times.
There are few benches and little shade, so rest in the cathedral or a nearby cafe at midday and come back in the evening.
The plaza is crowded in the evening, so watch out for pickpockets and lost phones, and carry valuables in front of you.
Fountain times and event schedules can change, so the information in this guide is for reference.
Repairs on the cathedral and construction screens may block some views.
During typhoon season (August–October), programs may be canceled and travel may be disrupted.
Kalesa fares are negotiated, so settle the price first.
Late in the evening, avoid dimly lit side streets.
You can politely decline carriage drivers and street vendors who call out around the plaza; ask the price first.
The whole old town of the UNESCO World Heritage city of
Vigan
spreads out around the plaza. Calle Crisologo, the cathedral and the museums are all within walking distance.
A branch of the National Museum a few minutes' walk from the plaza, with exhibits on Father José Burgos and Ilocos history.
A signature street food you can try at restaurants and shops around the old town.
Vigan empanada
is a good snack while strolling.
Heading north, you reach
Paoay Church
in Ilocos Norte. Confirm the travel time locally.
